```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

### Setup and path to data

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("cowplot")

# Point this at the run you want to report on, e.g. "output/2024-10-17_14-57-25",
# or set SEGTRACK_RUN in the environment before knitting.
run.dir <- Sys.getenv("SEGTRACK_RUN", unset = "output/<timestamp>")
data.dir <- run.dir
output.dir <- run.dir

pdir <- function(dirname, filename) {
  paste(dirname, filename, sep = "/")
}
```

### Read the segtrack summary

```{r}
tracks <- read.csv(pdir(data.dir, "all_traps_summary.csv")) %>%
  
  # add some useful features to the df
  mutate(trap_gID = paste(trap_nb, Global_id, sep = '_')) %>%
  group_by(Global_id) %>%
  mutate(track_length = length(frame)) %>%
  ungroup()
```

### Histogram of track lengths

```{r}
tracks %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = track_length)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

### Histogram of track lengths for different cell Types (mothers, trapped non-mothers, outsiders)
It looks like the mother cells have the longest track lengths which is consistent with them being the ones that are trapped for the longest times.
Question for Nadia: how is the mother defined again? I've forgotten.

```{r}
tracks %>%
  group_by(Global_id) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = track_length)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_wrap(~Type)
```

### Thresholding mother cells by track length to focus on ones that are trapped for a long time
Most outsiders have track lengths < 160 so seems to make sense to threshold here to increase chances of analysing well tracked mother cells.

```{r}
tracks %>%
  filter(Type == 'mother') %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = track_length)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 160, colour = "red")
```

### Plotting the dispersion index trajectories from the fluorescence channels for individual mother cells
```{r}
tracks %>%
  filter(fluor_max >= 0, Type == 'mother', track_length > 160) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = frame, y = (fluor_std^2 / fluor_avg))) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~trap_gID)
```

### Plot dispersion index for all mothers in one plot
```{r}
tracks %>%
  filter(fluor_max >= 0, Type == 'mother', track_length > 160) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = frame, y = (fluor_std^2 / fluor_avg), colour = trap_gID)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_cowplot()
```

### Plot average fluorescence for all mothers in one plot
Here you can see we probably need background subtraction and flicker correction but it's also interesting that the population becomes more heterogeneous as it ages. Would be cool to test if this is general and whether it could give the population a competitive advantage.

```{r}
tracks %>%
  filter(fluor_max >= 0, Type == 'mother', track_length > 160) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = frame, y = (fluor_avg), colour = trap_gID)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_cowplot()
```

Here it would be good to check around frame 150 to make sure that some IDs didn't switch and cause the drops in fluorescence.

### Workaround to get cell size from number of fluorescent pixels
We should really extract size from the mask as this would give us more measurements and always allow size to be measured even in experiments without fluorescence.

```{r}
mutated <- tracks %>% filter(fluor_max > 0)

mutated$size <- str_length(mutated$fluorescence_values)

mutated %>%
  filter(fluor_max >= 0, Type == 'mother', track_length > 160) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = frame, y = (size))) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~trap_gID)
```
### Average cell size

```{r}
mutated %>%
  filter(fluor_max >= 0, Type == 'mother', track_length > 160) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = frame - first_frame, y = (size))) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_cowplot()
```


### Looking at the centroids of the mother cells over time

```{r}

tracks %>%
  filter(Type == 'mother') %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Centroid_x, y = Centroid_y, colour = frame, group = trap_gID)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .2) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  theme_cowplot() +
  facet_wrap(~trap_gID)
```

```{r}
tracks %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Centroid_x, y = Centroid_y, colour = Type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d() +
  theme_cowplot()
```

### Is there a way we can get an idea of age?
Daughter cells are probably going to move in the x direction as they fly out of the traps. Looking at overview it seems that the daughters are not tracked well e.g. often two different daughters are assigned the same ID.

```{r}
tracks %>%
  filter(trap_nb == 27) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = frame, y = Centroid_x, colour = Type, group = Global_id)) +
  geom_line()
```

### Potential improvements
For some reason, the template matching isn't working perfectly, so some cells get left out.

![Template matching eample](/Users/ucbtpes/yeast_segtrack_pipeline/output/2024-06-19_10-32-19/detected_traps_using_TM_CCOEFF_NORMED.png)
The threshold variable is located in template_matching.py file line 189. Try modifying that.

Another potential improvement would be to have an option for multiple fluorescence channels.    

### Further testing
A good test case would be the splicing reporter. This can be found in Mihailo's ageing chip directory on the server named: 20210426_16157... The WT strain is 16157 and the first 10 positions. I think this might be Anne's data originally?

- I found template matching works on 8-bit images but not on 16-bit for some reason. Perhaps there should be a check/prompt to make sure images are 8-bit before starting..? Segmentation worked fine on 16-bit so it was just a matter of repeating without segmentation. Segmentation/tracking has an error if you use 8bit images so best to use 16bit raw data.

- Note that 2024-10-17 template matching works fine on a nice looking movie that is 16-bit so the above isn't true. Perhaps it just helps when the movie is poor quality.

- Trying to rotate the movie to have the traps on their sides made it substantially worse.

- Manually lowered threshold for templating matching from 0.7 to 0.6 (template_matching.py file line 189).

- tracking really did not work so well for this... Why? Will have to manually correct.
